notes.47.1: 'incredundas' is a doubtful form; taken as 'incredible' ('not to be believed'). The reference is to the Twelve Tables' ban on charming a neighbour's crops away.
notes.38.1: The thirteen terms in the list, and zōotoka/ōotoka, are Greek in the original (Apuleius's point is that he coined Latin for them); kept in transliteration with glosses.
notes.90.1: The edition marks the word 'his' before Moses as corrupt (†); it is left as it stands. Carmendas I cannot identify; Iohannes is probably the Jannes of the Moses legend.

nodes.text: For if, as I read in a great many authors, a magus in the Persian language is what a priest is in ours, what crime is it, after all, to be a priest and to know duly, to understand and to be skilled in the laws of ceremonies, the proper order of rites, the law of religious observance — if indeed magic is what Plato explains it to be when he records in which disciplines the Persians train a boy growing up to be king? I remember the very words of that divine man; go over them with me, Maximus: 'When the boy has reached twice seven years, those whom they call the royal tutors take him in charge. These are four men chosen from among the Persians, judged the best of those in their prime: the wisest, the most just, the most temperate and the bravest. Of these, one teaches the magic of Zoroaster son of Oromazes, and this is the worship of the gods; he also teaches the arts of kingship.'

Do you hear, you who rashly accuse it, that magic is an art acceptable to the immortal gods, fully versed in how to worship and revere them, pious, of course, and knowing in things divine, renowned ever since Zoroaster and Oromazes, its founders, a high priestess of the heavenly powers? Indeed it is taught among the first lessons of kingship, and among the Persians no one is lightly allowed to be a magus, any more than to be king. The same Plato, in another dialogue, left this in writing about a certain Zalmoxis, a man of Thracian race but of the same art: 'and that the charms are the fair words.' If that is so, why should I not be allowed to know either the good words of Zalmoxis or the priestly lore of Zoroaster? But if these men, after the common fashion, think the true magus to be one who, through converse with the immortal gods, has the power to do all the incredible things he wishes by some force of incantations, I am utterly amazed that they were not afraid to accuse a man whom they admit to be so powerful. For so hidden and divine a power cannot be guarded against in the same way as other things. Whoever summons an assassin to court comes with an escort; whoever accuses a poisoner eats more cautiously; whoever charges a thief guards his belongings. But whoever brings a magus of the kind these men describe into peril of his life — with what escort, what precautions, what guards could he ward off a ruin unseen and inescapable? With none, of course; and so to bring a charge of that kind is not the act of a man who believes in it.

But these charges are generally thrown at philosophers through a kind of common error of the ignorant: some of them, those who search out the pure and simple causes of bodies, they consider irreligious and so say they deny the gods, such as Anaxagoras and Leucippus and Democritus and Epicurus and the other champions of natural philosophy; others, however, who investigate the providence of the world more searchingly and honour the gods more devotedly, these the crowd calls magi, as if they also knew how to make happen what they know does happen, as once were Epimenides and Orpheus and Pythagoras and Ostanes; and afterwards, in the same way, the Purifications of Empedocles, the *daemonion* [divine sign] of Socrates, and the Good of Plato were held suspect. I congratulate myself, then, that I too am numbered among so many and such great men.

You have heard, Maximus, things most of which you had, of course, read in the ancient philosophers. And remember that these volumes were written by me about fishes alone: which of them are begotten by mating, which grow together out of mud; how often and at what time of year the females of each of their kinds come into heat and the males into rut; by what organs and for what reasons nature has distinguished the viviparous among them from the oviparous — for so I call in Latin what the Greeks call *zōotoka* and *ōotoka* — and, not to go laboriously through the generation of animals, then about their differences and diet and organs and ages and a great many other things, necessary indeed to know, but out of place in a court. I shall also have a few passages read from my Latin writings that concern the same expertise, in which you will notice both things worth recording and rarely known, and also names unused by the Romans and, so far as I know, uncoined to this day; yet these names, by my labour and study, come over from the Greek in such a way that they are nevertheless struck in Latin coinage. Or let your advocates, Aemilianus, tell us where they have read these terms expressed in Latin. I shall speak about water creatures alone, and touch on the other animals only in the differences they share. Listen, then, to what I shall say. Presently you will shout that I am reciting magical names in the Egyptian or Babylonian manner: *selacheia* [cartilaginous fishes], *malakeia* [soft-bodied creatures], *malakostraka* [soft-shelled creatures], *chondrakantha* [gristle-spined], *ostrakoderma* [shell-skinned], *karcharodonta* [saw-toothed], *amphibia* [living in both elements], *lepidōta* [scaled], *pholidōta* [plated], *dermoptera* [skin-winged], *steganopoda* [web-footed], *monērē* [solitary], *synagelastika* [shoaling] — I could even go on; but it is not worth wasting the day on these, so that I may have time to move on to the rest. Meanwhile, read out these few that I have named, as I rendered them in Latin. —

Now, since these men's fishes have been sufficiently exposed, hear another charge, of equal stupidity indeed, but devised many times more emptily and more wickedly. They knew themselves that the fish argument was futile and would come to nothing, and besides that its novelty was laughable (for who ever heard tell of fish being scaled and boned for magical sorceries?), and that they had better invent something from matters more widely known and also believed. So, following the pattern of popular opinion and rumour, they made up a story that a certain boy, enchanted with a spell, with onlookers sent away, in a secret place, with a little altar and a lamp and a few accomplices as witnesses, fell down where he had been enchanted, and was afterwards roused not knowing himself. Nor did they dare to go any further with the lie; yet for the story to be complete, this too ought to have been added: that the same boy foretold many things by prophecy. For this is the profit we are told chants bring, presage and divination; and this marvel concerning boys is confirmed not only by popular opinion but also by the authority of learned men. I remember reading in Varro the philosopher, a most precisely learned and erudite man, both other things of the same kind and this too: that when the people of Tralles were consulting by magical inquiry about the outcome of the Mithridatic war, a boy gazing at an image of Mercury in water sang in a hundred and sixty verses what was to come. And likewise that Fabius, when he had lost five hundred denarii, came to consult Nigidius; that boys inspired by him with a spell revealed where the purse had been buried with part of them, and how the rest had been dispersed; and that one denarius of that sum was even held by Marcus Cato the philosopher, who admitted that he had received it from an attendant as an offering to Apollo.

These and other things about magic and boys I do read in many authors, but I am of two minds whether to say it can happen or to deny it, although I believe Plato that between gods and men, intermediate in nature and in place, there are set certain divine powers, and that these govern all divinations and the marvels of the magi; indeed I also reflect that the human soul, especially a child's and a simple one, may, whether through the diversion of chants or the soothing of scents, be lulled to sleep and carried away into forgetfulness of present things, and, the memory of the body being for a little while removed, be brought back and return to its own nature, which is, of course, immortal and divine, and so, as if in a kind of sleep, foretell the future. But truly, however that may be, if any credence is to be given to such things, that prophetic boy, whoever he is, ought, so far as I hear, to be chosen handsome and sound in body, quick in mind and fluent in speech, so that either the divine power may lodge worthily in him as in a good house — if indeed it is enclosed in a boy's body — or the soul itself, once awakened, may quickly be brought back to its own power of divination, which, being readily implanted in it and neither wounded nor dulled by any forgetfulness, may easily be taken up again. For, as Pythagoras used to say, a Mercury should not be carved from just any wood. If that is so, name who that boy was — healthy, unblemished, clever, handsome — whom I deemed worthy of initiating with a spell. But Thallus, whom you named, has need of a doctor rather than a magus; for the poor wretch is so worn down by epilepsy that three or four times a day, often, without any incantations, he falls down and wears out all his limbs with convulsions; his face is ulcerous, his forehead and the back of his head battered, his eyes dull, his nostrils gaping, his feet unsteady. The greatest magus of all is he in whose presence Thallus has stayed standing for long: so constantly does he droop and sink with the disease as if with sleep.

Or why were you demanding that so large a household be produced? Accusing me of magic, you served notice concerning fifteen slaves: what if you were accusing me of violence — how many slaves, pray, would you demand? So fifteen slaves know something, and it is secret? Or is it not secret, and yet magical? You must admit one or the other of these: either that a thing in which I did not fear so many accomplices was not unlawful, or, if it was unlawful, that so many accomplices ought not to have known of it. This magic, as far as I hear, is a matter consigned to the laws, forbidden already from ancient times by the Twelve Tables because of incredible charms for luring away crops; therefore it is no less secret than foul and horrible, generally kept up through the nights, hidden in darkness, withdrawn from witnesses and murmured in chants; at it few are present, not only of slaves but even of free men: and you want fifteen slaves to have been present? Was that a wedding, or some other well-attended ceremony, or a banquet begun early? Do fifteen slaves take part in a magical rite as if they were the Fifteen Men appointed for performing sacred rites? But for what purpose would I have brought in so many, if they are too many to share a secret? Fifteen free men are a public assembly, as many slaves a household, as many in chains a slave-prison. Or was their number needed for help, to hold the victims of purification for a long time? But you have named no victims except hens. Or was it to count the grains of incense, or to throw Thallus down?

Your third lie was that the figure of a dreadful corpse had been made, emaciated or completely disembowelled, utterly horrible and ghostly. If you had found out so evident a sign of magic, why did you not serve notice on me to produce it? Was it so that you could lie freely about something not present? Yet the means for that falsehood has been taken from you by a happy feature of my habits. For it is my custom, wherever I go, to carry the image of some god stored among my books, and on feast days to pray to it with incense and unmixed wine, and sometimes with victims. So a while ago, when I heard it repeatedly called a skeleton in a most shameless lie, I ordered someone to run and fetch from my lodging the little Mercury that Saturninus here made for me at Oea. Hand it to me, you; let them see it, hold it, examine it. There you are: the thing that scoundrel called a skeleton. Do you hear the outcry of everyone present? Do you hear the condemnation of your lie? Are you not ashamed at last of so many false charges? Is this the skeleton, is this the ghost, is this what you kept calling a demon? Is that a magical image, or a customary and ordinary one? Take it, I beg you, Maximus, and look at it; it is well that a consecrated object should be handed to hands as pure and as pious as yours. Look: how handsome its face is and full of the bloom of the wrestling-ground, how cheerful the god's expression, how becomingly the down spreads over the cheeks on either side, how the curled hair shows on the head beneath the lowest edge of the cap's brim, how charmingly the matching little wings stand out above the temples, and how gracefully the garment is gathered round the shoulders. Whoever dares to call this a skeleton surely either sees no images of the gods or neglects them all; and whoever thinks it a ghost is himself ghost-ridden.

I let these things go. I come now to the very root of the accusation, to the very motive for the sorcery. Let Aemilianus and Rufinus answer: for what gain, even if I were ever so much a magus, would I have lured Pudentilla into marriage with spells and potions? And I know that many men arraigned for some crime, even when it was proved that there had been some motive, have nevertheless defended themselves amply with this one point: that their life was far removed from crimes of this kind, and that it should not count against them that there appear to have been certain inducements to wrongdoing; for not everything that could have been done is to be taken as done; the turns of events fall out variously; the sure indicator is each man's character, which, being always disposed with the same temper toward virtue or toward malice, is a firm argument for accepting a charge or rejecting it. Although I could rightly say this, I make you a present of it, and I do not think it enough to have fully cleared myself of all that you have alleged unless I have nowhere allowed even the slightest suspicion of magic to stand. Consider for yourselves with what confidence in my innocence and with what contempt for you I am acting: if a single reason, even the smallest, is found why I should have sought marriage with Pudentilla for some advantage of my own, if you prove any gain however modest, then let me be that famous Carmendas, or Damigeron, or † his Moses, or Iohannes, or Apollobex, or Dardanus himself, or whoever else has been celebrated among the magi since Zoroaster and Ostanes.
